nodes.html:
For as long as I've been brewing, the process has always been a mix of equal parts science, patience, and a fair bit of trial and error. It's a rewarding journey, but as the experiments get more ambitious and the batches more frequent, the costs of quality ingredients—honey, yeast, grains, and fruits—start to add up.

To keep the momentum going and accelerate the pace of these experiments, I've decided to open up a way for those of you who enjoy the recipes and findings to contribute.

Why Support the Brew?

Brewing isn't just about following a recipe; it's about the pursuit of the perfect profile. To get there, I'm constantly testing different variables: varying honey sources, experimenting with nutrient timings, and trying out unique fruit additions.

By helping cover the cost of ingredients, you're directly fueling this research. My goal is to push the boundaries of what's possible in a home setup and, most importantly, to share every single finding—the triumphs and the "learning experiences"—with all of you.

What Your Support Enables

Every contribution goes directly back into the carboys. Specifically, your support helps with:

  • Quality Ingredients: Sourcing higher-grade honey and specialized yeast strains.
  • Diverse Experiments: Trying out expensive fruits or rare additives that I might otherwise skip.
  • Consistent Documentation: Allowing me to dedicate more time to outlining the findings and sharing detailed guides here on the blog.

How to Contribute

If you'd like to help keep the fermentation flowing, you can support me via Ko-fi:

Support the Brewing Journey on Ko-fi

Whether it's the cost of a single jar of honey or a larger contribution to a complex batch, every bit makes a tangible difference in how quickly we can test new theories and share the results.

Thank you for being part of this journey and for supporting the craft. Let's see what we can brew next.

frontmatter.title: Fueling the Fermentation: Supporting the Brewing Journey
frontmatter.author: Joseph Crawford

Bottling is the most rewarding—and potentially most stressful—part of the brewing process. After weeks of waiting, your brew finally moves from the fermenter into its final home. It is also the stage where a few careless mistakes can turn a promising batch into broken glass and a sticky floor, so I treat it with the same care as the earlier steps.

The Setup: Getting the Liquid into the Bottle

There are several ways to approach bottling, and the "right" one usually depends on your gear and your tolerance for mess.

The Spigot and Hose

If your fermenter has a built-in spigot, the simplest path is to attach a food-grade hose and run it directly into each bottle. The main drawback is flow control: the liquid keeps moving whenever the spigot is open, so you often lose product while shifting the hose from bottle to bottle. Technically, you can close the spigot between bottles, but I try to avoid that. The spigot sits close to the lees at the bottom, and repeatedly opening and closing it tends to stir up sediment and cloud the finished brew.

The Auto-Siphon and Bottle Filler

For a cleaner operation, I use an auto-siphon to move liquid out of the fermenter, connected to a bottle-filling wand that controls flow into each bottle. The wand has a small plastic tip at the bottom that acts like a valve: press it against the bottom of a bottle and liquid flows; lift it and the flow stops. This lets me move from bottle to bottle with minimal waste, losing only a drop or two rather than a stream of mead or wine.

The Critical Safety Check: Avoiding "Bottle Bombs"

Before a single drop enters a bottle, you must be certain fermentation is finished. I verify this by taking multiple gravity readings over several days until the number is stable. If the yeast is still active and you seal it in glass with residual sugar, you risk a bottle bomb — the internal pressure climbs until the bottle fails, sending glass shards and sticky liquid across your storage area.

Once fermentation is confirmed complete, you need to stabilize the brew. I use two different methods, depending on the batch: chemical stabilization with powders, or pasteurization with heat. They are not interchangeable, and each changes the timing of other steps like back-sweetening.

Chemical Stabilization

I add a combination of potassium metabisulfite and potassium sorbate to stop the yeast from restarting fermentation. For a standard one-gallon batch, I use approximately 1/4 teaspoon of potassium metabisulfite and 1/2 teaspoon of potassium sorbate. The metabisulfite works as an antioxidant and antimicrobial, while the sorbate keeps any remaining yeast cells from multiplying. I mix them in thoroughly and wait at least 24 hours before adding more sugar or bottling.

Pasteurization

The other reliable method is pasteurization, which uses heat to neutralize the yeast. When I choose this route, I follow the most common homebrewing standards: hold the bottles at either 140°F for 20 minutes or 160°F for 1 minute.

The key detail is that these temperatures must be the internal temperature of the liquid, not just the water surrounding the bottles. I use my all-in-one Clawhammer supply system to heat water to 160°F, then set the bottles in my grain basket. That setup lets me stick a thermometer directly into one of the bottles so I can track the actual liquid temperature and stop the process once the target is reached, without boiling the brew.

Back-sweetening

If the finished brew tastes too dry, you can back-sweeten with honey or another sugar source. Timing matters here, because adding sugar to active yeast will restart fermentation.

When using Potassium Sorbate + Potassium Metabisulfite:

Fermentation finishes → Rack off the lees → Add stabilizers → Wait 24–48 hours → Back-sweeten → Verify stability → Bottle.

When using Pasteurization:

Fermentation finishes → Back-sweeten → Allow honey to fully dissolve and mix → Pasteurize → Cool → Bottle.

The critical distinction: do not rely on potassium sorbate alone. The sorbate and metabisulfite work together, and neither replaces the need to confirm fermentation is truly finished before you add more sugar.

Bottle Carbonation with Crown Caps

If you want a sparkling finish, you can bottle carbonate using standard beer bottles and crown caps. Carbonation requires leaving a precise amount of residual sugar — called priming sugar — in the liquid. The yeast consumes that sugar inside the sealed bottle and produces CO2 that dissolves into the brew.

Using crown caps is the gold standard here because they form a true airtight seal that can withstand the high pressures involved. For a single 12-ounce bottle, I target about 2 grams of white sugar (roughly 1/2 teaspoon), scaling proportionally for larger bottles.

There are many calculators available to determine the exact amount of priming sugar based on your volume and desired carbonation level. One tool I have used is the Brewers Friend Priming Calculator.

Some brewers add sugar to each bottle individually; others dissolve the full amount in the bulk container before bottling. If you use the bulk method, make sure the sugar is fully dissolved and evenly mixed before you start siphoning, or you will end up with some bottles flat and others over-carbonated.

Whichever route you choose, keep your priming calculations exact. Too little sugar and the brew is flat; too much and you are back to the "bottle bomb" scenario.

I bought a Tilt Hydrometer because the idea of watching fermentation gravity from my phone sounded like the future. No more sanitizing a wine thief, no more sticky hydrometer cylinders, no more guessing when a batch had stalled. Just drop the device into the must, open the app, and watch the numbers roll in. In practice, that fantasy is about seventy percent real.

What the Tilt Does Well

The Tilt really is clever. It is a sealed, floating hydrometer and thermometer that broadcasts gravity and temperature over Bluetooth. Sanitize it, drop it in, and it starts logging. For someone who makes mead and wine in small batches, the convenience is meaningful. I can check a fermentation curve from the kitchen table, the office, or even while running errands if I have cloud logging enabled.

Setup is genuinely simple. The device arrives pre-calibrated, and the app finds it quickly. There are no probes to insert, no grommets to wrestle into a lid, and no risk of introducing oxygen every time I want a reading. That alone makes it attractive for long secondary ferments where you want to peek without disturbing anything.

Tilt also offers the units in multiple colors, which is genuinely useful if you run more than one fermenter at a time. Each color shows up as its own device in the app, so I can tell at a glance which bucket is which. For a small-scale home brewer juggling a couple of projects, that little detail matters.

The Caveats I Did Not Expect

For all the polish in the marketing, the day-to-day experience has rough edges. The first one showed up before I even brewed with it: the battery drains on the shelf. I store my Tilt upright, sideways, and every other orientation people suggest online, and it still shows up weaker than I expect the next time I need it. It is not a dealbreaker because the battery is replaceable, but it is annoying for a device whose whole pitch is readiness.

The second issue is specific to beer, and it is the one that makes me hesitate before dropping the Tilt into a hoppy or high-protein batch. Krausen can build up enough that the Tilt no longer tilts freely. When that happens, the reading lags or flatlines, and you are left trying to decide whether fermentation is done or the device is just stuck against the side of the bucket. In wines and meads with less aggressive foam it has been more reliable, but I have learned not to trust it blindly in the final days of any batch.

One Idea for a Better Design

I have wondered whether a simple mechanical rig could solve the krausen problem. The sketch below is just a thought experiment, not something I have built or tested, but it shows the idea: a small rectangular chassis holds the Tilt on a pivot so it can still rock and measure gravity, while an adjustable cord and a ballast weight keep the whole assembly submerged below the foam layer.

If a design like this kept the sensor below the surface while still allowing it to tilt, it could remove one of the biggest accuracy problems the Tilt has today. Whether Tilt or a third-party accessory maker ever produces something similar is another question entirely.

Then there is the software experience. The data exports to Google Sheets, which works, but it does not feel like a modern product dashboard. Graphs are janky, layout is manual, and there is no beautiful Tilt-owned portal that ties everything together. For a premium brewing accessory, the reporting side feels like an afterthought. I would love a clean web portal with shareable batch timelines, but that does not exist today.

Finally, I simply use it less than I thought I would. For meads and wines, gravity often follows a predictable arc, and once I have a rhythm I do not feel compelled to log every point digitally. I still use the Tilt for experiments or finicky batches, but it is not the default tool I imagined it would be.

Is It Worth Buying?

Honestly, I do not think it is. The Tilt Hydrometer has its strengths, but once you stack the $135 price against the inaccurate readings, the janky graphs, and the general sense that the software has been neglected, it starts to feel like an overpriced gimmick rather than an essential brewing tool.

I worry it is heading the same direction as the PLAATO Airlock, which I also bought. PLAATO looked promising, then the company announced it was shifting focus to commercial breweries and away from consumers. The app stopped getting updates, the cloud service effectively vanished, and the device I paid good money for became a paperweight overnight. It remains one of the worst purchases I have ever made. I look at the Tilt and ask the same question: is the product going to keep improving, or is the consumer side going to be abandoned once the next pivot happens?

Right now the hardware has potential, but the software and ecosystem do not inspire confidence. A small weighted chassis that holds the Tilt below the surface while still letting it tilt freely would solve the krausen-sticking problem almost entirely. If Tilt commits to that kind of hardware refinement and a real reporting platform, this could become a solid investment. Until then, I would not recommend buying one for most homebrewers.

Rating: 3 out of 5 — a neat idea with real utility, but at this price it needs accuracy and software that keep up with the marketing.

frontmatter.excerpt: The Tilt Hydrometer promises 24/7 gravity and temperature readings straight from your fermenter. I wanted to love it, and in some ways I do—but a few persistent flaws keep it from earning a permanent place in every batch.

My brewing journey started in 2022, though I'd actually started researching the topic during COVID. After falling down countless YouTube rabbit holes, I was pretty knowledgeable on the subject before I ever brewed my first batch.

I've since added a dedicated brewing section to the site where I share recipes for beer, wine, and mead — complete with ingredients, step-by-step instructions, and notes from my own brewing experiences.

Learning From the Pros

I started watching YouTube videos to learn the basics. I call it YouTube Academy — because you can literally learn anything you want from YouTube, and brewing is no exception. Three channels became my go-to resources:

  • Man Made Mead — The definitive guide to all things mead
  • Doin' The Most — Creative recipes and experiments
  • City Steading Brews — Practical brewing for urban dwellers

These creators made brewing approachable. They broke down complex processes into simple steps and showed that you didn't need a massive setup to make great beverages.

The Northern Brewer Starter Kit

Following their recommendations, I bought a 1-gallon mead kit from Northern Brewer. This seems to be the universal entry point for new brewers — and I suspect that's not accidental. Northern Brewer was heavily sponsoring content creators at the time, providing them with tools and ingredients for their videos. Smart marketing, and it definitely worked on me.

The kit arrived with everything I needed to make my first beer: Caribou Slobber, a brown ale extract kit. The beer came out decent, but it wasn't a good first brewing experience. It wasn't really an enjoyable brown ale — and I've enjoyed brown ales in the past.

My second kit was a 1-gallon elderberry mead kit. The mead came out nice, but I messed it up by over-sweetening when I back-sweetened it — the entire batch was ruined. After those experiences, I started thinking about expanding.

Moving to Beer

At this point in my life, I enjoyed drinking beer way more than wine, and mead was an entirely new category for me. I wanted to brew what I actually liked to drink. Beer felt like the logical next step — more complex recipes, more variables to control, and a much wider range of styles to explore.

When I started brewing beer, I turned to a new set of YouTube creators for knowledge:

  • Adam Makes Beer
  • Beer-N-BBQ by Larry
  • Bitter Reality Brewing
  • Cityscape Brewing
  • Clawhammer Supply
  • David Heath Homebrew
  • Don Osborn
  • Exit 12 Homebrew
  • Hops & Gnarly

I also followed these creators who have since stopped making brewing content:

  • Jus' Brewing
  • Party Time Brewing
  • Short Circuited Brewers

Leveling Up

My wonderful wife saw how much I was enjoying the hobby and surprised me with a serious upgrade — a 10 gallon electric brewing system from Clawhammer Supply. This was a massive step up from my 1-gallon stovetop setup. Digital temperature control, built-in pump, and enough capacity to brew real batches that would actually last more than a week.

It was exactly what I needed to take brewing from a fun experiment to a serious hobby.

The Bottling Problem

I was able to brew a batch of beer but had no easy way to store it when finished. I was having to bottle up around 48 bottles of beer after every batch — cleaning, sanitizing, filling, capping, and then finding space to store them all. It turned every brew day into a two-day affair with all the cleanup and bottling.

Bottling is something that I do not miss.

The Honda Dealership Connection

The real pivot point came unexpectedly. We went to our local Honda dealership to trade in our minivan — my wife was done being a soccer mom and wanted an SUV. We ended up driving home in a 2020 Honda Pilot, but that's not the real story here.

While we were there, I struck up a conversation with the sales manager. We got a bit off-topic from the vehicle, and I mentioned I was getting into home brewing. He was surprised — not at the fact that I was a home brewer, but rather that I brought up the topic at his workplace. As it turned out, he was selling a bunch of brewing equipment because he'd lost time for the hobby.

"What do you have?" I asked.

He had a full keezer with kegs, taps, CO₂ tank, regulator — everything I needed to have beer on tap in my kitchen. He also had a beer gun for bottle filling, two large 5-gallon plastic fermenters, and other odds and ends for brewing.

I asked how much he wanted for it. When he said approximately $1,000, I quickly stated that I couldn't take that on along with the vehicle. But looking back, it was well worth what he was asking — a complete setup like that would have cost significantly more buying everything new.

That's when my wife injected herself into the conversation.

"No, you have to buy this," she said firmly. "This is something you have wanted for a while, and opportunities like this do not come up that often."

She was right, of course. I'd been dreaming about having beer on tap at home since I started brewing, but I never thought I'd find a complete setup — especially not from a random conversation at a car dealership.

In the end, we walked out with the vehicle along with a date to pick up the brewing equipment.

What I've Brewed

Over the years I've brewed a few different styles of beer. I started off using an all-grain kit from Northern Brewer but found that shipping delays caused me some issues. Something was happening at Northern Brewer that was causing long delays — I'm not sure what was going on behind the scenes, but waiting weeks for ingredients got frustrating fast.

I ended up switching suppliers shortly after that experience. I started using More Beer, which has never given me any issues over the years. Reliable shipping, good quality ingredients, and their customer service has been solid.

I've made an IPA, a Cream Ale, and a Summer Shandy — but I tend to stick to what I like to brew. Over the years that's been cream ales. They're crisp, clean, refreshing, and a crowd-pleaser when I have friends over. Not too hoppy, not too heavy — just an easy-drinking beer that works year-round.

I'm also planning to try making my own hard seltzer — it's a simple recipe of just corn sugar, water, yeast, and flavoring.

Full Circle

More recently I've had limited time to brew beer. Maybe this time limitation has something to do with it, but I've started making more wine and meads again.

I currently have a Cherry Mead in primary fermentation — a sweet mead with whole frozen cherries added in both primary and secondary for depth of flavor and that beautiful red color.

It's funny how things come full circle. I started with mead, moved to beer when I had the time and equipment, and now find myself back to mead as life gets busier. Different phases, different beverages, same satisfying hobby.

frontmatter.title: My Home Brewing Journey: From Mead to Beer on Tap
frontmatter.excerpt: How I started home brewing in 2022 with a 1-gallon mead kit and ended up with a full keezer setup in my kitchen thanks to a chance encounter at a Honda dealership.

Notes

This is a live batch — started on July 22, 2026. This post will be updated as the mead progresses through each stage. Check back for updates on the cherry bag removal, secondary fermentation, bottling, final gravity, ABV, and tasting notes once it's drinking ready.

frontmatter.title: Cherry Mead
frontmatter.excerpt: A sweet cherry mead made with Maker's Mark Premium Wildflower Honey, whole frozen cherries, and Red Star Premier Blanc yeast. Primary fermentation with fruit in a mesh bag, then a second cherry addition in secondary for flavor and color.
frontmatter.author: joseph-crawford

nodes.html:
Lessons for Next Time

This batch taught me several things I will do differently next time:

  • Take an original gravity reading. Without an OG I cannot calculate ABV, which is useful information for labeling and sharing the recipe.
  • Measure back-sweetening additions. Eyeballing the honey left me with no reproducible data. Next batch I will weigh the honey before and after adding it.
  • Keep better yeast notes. I recorded Red Star Premier Cote Des Blancs for this batch, but on future batches I will also write down the exact nutrient schedule and any other additions.

frontmatter.title: Blackberry Mead
frontmatter.excerpt: A deep purple blackberry mead started without an original gravity reading, fermented to dryness, then sweetened back and bottle-pasteurized. Lessons learned from a first attempt.

nodes.html:
Notes

This dandelion mead is ready to drink immediately after bottling — no bottle aging required.

The fermentation was remarkably straightforward. Red Star Premier Côte is a reliable yeast that ferments cleanly and flocculates well, leaving behind a mead that's bright and easy to drink.

About the photos: I don't have many images of this brew because I threw it together quickly once I had the flowers deconstructed. The process was impromptu — once the petals were separated from the stems, everything moved fast.

 

Tasting Notes

The finished mead pours a pale golden color with excellent clarity. The nose carries distinct floral notes — partly from the Ambrosia honey, partly from the dandelion tea. On the palate, it's lightly sweet with a dry finish. The dandelion contributes an herbal, almost tea-like quality that makes this mead feel both rustic and refined. It's refreshing served slightly chilled.

frontmatter.title: Dandelion Mead
frontmatter.excerpt: A bright, floral mead made with foraged dandelion flowers and Ambrosia honey. The dandelion tea brings a subtle herbal quality that pairs beautifully with the honey's sweetness.
frontmatter.author: joseph-crawford

nodes.html:
Awaiting the Taste Test

Now these bottles will go on the shelf until one year has passed, at which point I will do a taste testing and update this post with the taste testing results.

Note on Secondary Fruit Addition: I considered adding fresh strawberries to secondary fermentation for more vibrant color and flavor, similar to the cherry mead technique. However, when I treated the original fruit with a Camden tablet, I noticed the strawberries turned from bright red to a muted pink — I suspect this chemical reaction would affect any fresh fruit added later as well. Additionally, since fresh strawberries carry wild yeast on their surfaces, adding them to secondary could introduce unwanted fermentation activity and alter the wine's flavor profile. I opted to keep the secondary phase fruit-free and let the wine develop from the single fruit addition in primary.

frontmatter.title: Strawberry Wine
frontmatter.excerpt: A fresh strawberry wine made with pureed strawberries and a unique Camden tablet treatment to eliminate wild yeast before fermentation.

I bought a PLAATO Airlock because the pitch was irresistible: a smart airlock that counted fermentation bubbles, estimated gravity, and sent updates to my phone. It was one of those products that felt like the future of homebrewing. No samples, no hydrometer readings, no guesswork. Just sanitize the bubbler, connect it to the app, and watch the fermentation curve build itself. For around $100, I expected a few years of useful data. I got a few months before the whole platform collapsed.

What It Was Supposed to Do

The idea was genuinely clever. Instead of opening the fermenter and pulling samples, the PLAATO Airlock measured CO₂ activity by counting bubbles through the airlock. That data fed into an app that tried to estimate gravity trends and fermentation completion. When it worked, it was the kind of tool that made you feel like you had a brewery dashboard in your pocket.

The hardware looked good too. A clean black unit with a minimalist Scandinavian design that fit into my fermenter setup without looking like a prototype. Setup was straightforward, the app paired quickly, and for the first few batches I actually enjoyed checking the graphs.

Where It Fell Apart

The problems started with silence. Firmware updates slowed, then stopped. The app began throwing connection errors that would clear up after a restart, then errors that would not clear up at all. Then came the announcement: PLAATO was pivoting to commercial brewing applications and would no longer support the homebrew community. Reading that message felt like being told your car manufacturer had decided to focus on fleet vehicles and was turning off every consumer car on the road.

Shortly after the announcement, the app stopped working entirely. The cloud APIs that the device relied on were sunsetted, and without those endpoints the airlock could not authenticate, sync, or display data. There was no local mode, no open-source bridge, no way to repurpose the hardware. The device still powers on, still blinks, still connects to Wi-Fi, and still measures nothing useful because the backend it depends on is gone.

What makes it worse is how the company handled it. There was no meaningful migration path, no refund program, no commitment to keeping existing customers functional. The messaging was corporate and evasive, as if abandoning the people who funded the product was just a strategic pivot. It was not a technical failure. It was a deliberate choice to render paid hardware useless.

Is It Worth Buying?

Absolutely not. Even if you find a used PLAATO Airlock for cheap, it is non-functional. There is no app worth installing, no cloud service feeding it data, and no developer community resurrecting it. It is a $100 plastic paperweight with a battery and a blinking light.

The PLAATO Airlock is the reason I now hesitate before buying any cloud-dependent brewing gadget. If a product needs someone else's server to stay alive, it is only as reliable as that company's business model. In this case, the business model changed, and every homebrew customer paid the price.

I would also caution any commercial brewers considering their current product line. If PLAATO was this quick to discard the homebrew community that funded their early growth, what is to say they will not pivot again and leave commercial operations without the tools and data they invested in? When a company treats its earliest adopters as disposable, it is a serious warning about long-term stability and commitment to any customer segment.

Rating: 1 out of 5 — a good idea destroyed by a company that treated its customers like disposable beta testers.

frontmatter.title: PLAATO Airlock Review
frontmatter.excerpt: The PLAATO Airlock promised smart fermentation tracking through a sleek bubbler. For a few months it worked. Then the company abandoned homebrewers, killed the app and API, and left every customer with useless hardware.
